items.title: 8 Creature Taming Games That Are Better Than Aniimo
items.summary: Aniimo is a great new creature taming game, but genre fans might enjoy these titles even more.
items.content:
By Aden Carter Published Sep 19, 2026, 4:30 PM EDT Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles.

Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant , XDA , Gamepur , Impulse Gamer , and WePC . He currently also works with GameSandwich and VideoGamer , where he handles guide content, news, and reviews for the latest games. Across his games writing career, he has worked as a freelance writer and editor, with experience reviewing around 40 games and interviewing multiple indie developers. Aden holds a B.A. in Creative Writing for Entertainment .

Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Aniimo is the latest in the collection of monster catching and taming games out there. The game gathered a lot of attention over the last year thanks to its cute design and fun aesthetic. Plus, it isn't every day that you get a game that is reminiscent of games like Pokémon.

You really missed out if you didn't have a Wii back in the day; these games changed the industry.

However, Aniimo is far from being the only monster-taming game out there. There are plenty of them that are worth trying out if you aren't afraid to delve into the far recesses of the Steam store.

There are older monster-taming titles that are great, and even newer ones that hold their own against Aniimo and even surpass it, so you should check out these games when you are tired of traversing Idyll.

Expand Collapse Slime Rancher 2 is one of those games where you don't really need to worry about combat. Instead, it is a creature-taming game that is more relaxed, allowing you to have more fun with exploration.

The world presented in the game is vast, giving you the ability to explore various biomes across a rather massive landscape. Your goal is to capture various slimes and start a farm with them.

You bring them home, place them in containment units, and watch them grow. You can then have them interact with other slimes to create new species. It is a weird science experiment of a game, but one that has a special quirk about it that you may absolutely love.

Ni no Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch Action RPG

Expand Collapse Are you a fan of Studio Ghibli? If you are, then you absolutely need to check out Ni No Kuni: Wrath of the White Witch , as the famed animation studio designed the cutscenes and had a major influence over the game's design.

Ni No Kuni places you in the shoes of Oliver — a young boy who travels to a fantasy realm after his mother is taken. As part of the game, you and your human companions can summon familiars to fight in battle.

Of course, the humans in the group can take part in combat as well. It is a cute and whimsical title that is very reminiscent of many of Studio Ghibli's movies, and one that is very memorable.

items.title: Aniimo challenged Pokémon and Palworld - the free-to-play online game exceeded 120,000 players
items.summary: Aniimo, a new competitor to Pokémon and Palworld, was released as a free-to-play game on Steam, PS5, and Xbox, attracting over 120,000 concurrent players.
items.content:
1 Источник: Steam 17 September 2026, 09:41 Dmitry Krivov Aniimo, a new competitor to Pokémon and Palworld, was released as a free-to-play game on Steam, PS5, and Xbox, attracting over 120,000 concurrent players.

The developers warn that the servers are currently overloaded, so connection issues and long queues are possible. Aniimo requires a constant internet connection.

Players have already left over 4,000 reviews on Steam, and only 60% of them are positive. Many complain about microtransactions that allow speeding up progress and obtaining cosmetic items. However, the developers promised not to use gacha mechanics when catching new creatures, and it seems this promise has been kept.

Aniimo's peak online concurrent players on Steam reached 127,914. For comparison, Palworld reached over 2 million concurrent users at launch.

On Xbox Series S, the game runs mostly stable at 60 FPS, although the frame rate sometimes drops to around 55 FPS. Gameplay from PS5 Pro has also been published.

items.summary: Some liken it to Infinity Nikki
items.content:

(Image credit: Pawprint Studio) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 3 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Aniimo, the stunning open-world creature collector unveiled at Summer Game Fest 2025 as part of the Xbox Games Showcase , is finally available to play on PC and consoles – but it's not proving too popular just yet.

Many of us Pokemon and Palworld fans were downright blown away by Pawprint Studio's adorable little creatures and vibrant visuals when Aniimo first came to light – heck, it's been on my wishlist since. The reviews so far, however, aren't exactly stellar. As of right now, the free-to-play game sits with a "Mixed" rating overall on Steam … and, yes, much of the more negative feedback has to do with microtransactions, purchases, and the like.

"Behind all the flashy visual flair is a mind-numbingly easy, boring gameplay loop built solely to push you toward aggressive monetization," reads one such review. "The sickening amount of predatory gacha mechanics and aggressive pay-to-win walls completely ruin any sense of genuine progression. Don't waste your time or money on this hollow cash-grab." Oof – and there are countless others like it, disappointingly enough.

Watch On One person writes, "It's very much a gacha game. When I see that you're able to spend money to obtain rare items and end-game Aniimo, it turned me away from the game. I don't mind paying for cosmetics or features that don't affect gameplay but it's disgusting how you're pushed to spend money here, so disappointed." Others slate Aniimo for its awkward writing and "hand-holding" – a complaint many modern games are no stranger to.

Not everyone finds Aniimo a disappointment, however. There are plenty of positive reviews, with fans celebrating the creature collector as an especially "cute" gem. I see quite a few comparisons to Infinity Nikki as well, with one review noting how Pawprint Studio's debut game is "giving Palworld x Infinity Nikki vibes." I'm personally sold on that, honestly… even if the whole microtransaction and gacha thing has me a bit wary.

Palworld 1.0 sees the game's biggest Steam player spike since its massive early access launch Beast of Reincarnation launches to mixed reviews on Steam and Metacritic, players divided on combat Palworld 1.0 is as much Elden Ring and Zelda inspired as it is Pokemon, but still enjoyable in its messiness Thankfully, Animo is free to download and try out. Furthermore, it's topping the charts even if its reception offers a mixed bag of negative and positive reviews – in fact, it's currently the sixth-most-played game on Steam, as per Valve's charts … so, yeah.

items.title: New Pokémon Competitor Launches With Over 100,000 Players on Steam
items.summary: Aniimo has launched with over 100,000 concurrent players on Steam, but the new Pokémon-like RPG is already receiving mixed reviews.
items.content:
Aniimo has launched with over 100,000 concurrent players on Steam, but the new Pokémon-like RPG is already receiving mixed reviews.

X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount{ display:none; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .discount .discount-tag{ line-height: 24px !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button.most-popular .join-now-button:hover { background: #000 !important; color: #fff !important; outline: 1px solid #fff !important; } .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button:hover { background: 0 0; outline: 1px solid rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); color: rgba(12, 12, 12, 1); } @media (max-width: 1220px){ .chargbee-tabs .tab-button .join-now-button { width: 100% !important; position: unset !important; } } A new creature-catching game called Aniimo has just been released, and the Pokémon-like RPG has already surpassed 100,000 concurrent players on Steam. Could this be the next Palworld to offer players an alternative to Pokémon?

Aniimo is a new open-world creature-catching RPG from Chinese developer Pawprint Studio. In the game, you explore a vast world and throw cubes at wild Aniimo to catch them before using the creatures in battle. Sounds a lot like Pokémon , right?

However, Aniimo puts its own spin on the familiar formula by allowing players to transform into their creatures. You can then directly control them to explore the world, complete traversal sections and solve puzzles.

Like Palworld , Aniimo appears to offer a fresh take on the catch ’em all genre. Despite only launching today, September 16, the game is already a hit on PC. According to SteamDB , Aniimo has surpassed 101,717 peak concurrent players on Steam . Considering it is still early morning across much of North America, that is pretty impressive!

It is difficult to say whether this will be the next Palworld , but Aniimo has already impressed Pokémon fans with its gorgeous visuals. However, despite its promising player count, not everyone is enjoying the new creature-catching RPG.

At the time of writing, Aniimo has a “Mixed” user rating on Steam. One of the biggest complaints is that the game reportedly adopts a gacha-like structure after its opening tutorial, with microtransactions and paid options that can speed up progression.

“Has such potential. Very good graphics, cool design of aniimo. However about an hour into the game you are bombarded with monthly passes, stores, objectives that you can bypass by paying, ways to speed up your levelling. Its very much a gatcha game,” one Steam user review reads. Another frustrated reviewer wrote: “Aniimo promised an authentic, gacha-free creature collector, but it delivers nothing more than a glorified digital storefront.”

It should be pointed out that the game does not require players to purchase these items. Not every review has been negative, either. One player wrote: “Im already loving how cute the aniimo and everything about this game is. It’s basically Palworld + Infinity Nikki! ”

While its Steam reviews are currently mixed, Aniimo is already off to a strong start based on how many people are playing it. Even if it does not reach the ridiculous heights of Palworld , this is another example of how much demand there is for new Pokémon-like games. And with Pokémon Winds and Waves still around a year and a half away, I totally get it.

items.title: New Palworld and Pokémon-like free-to-play creature collector Aniimo sees over 100k concurrent Steam players at launch, despite mixed reviews
items.summary: Aniimo has launched on September 16 for PC, Playstation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with the mobile version coming on September 23.
items.content:
Home News New Palworld and Pokémon-like free-to-play creature collector Aniimo sees over 100k concurrent Steam players at launch, despite mixed reviews Aniimo has launched on September 16 for PC, Playstation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, with the mobile version coming on September 23.

News 2026-09-16 18:13 Đorđe P Pawprint Interactive Entertainment released its free-to-play creature collector RPG Aniimo on September 16 for PC (Steam/Epic Games/official launcher), PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Android and iOS. The mobile version of the game is scheduled to release on September 23.

Aniimo is set in the open world of Idyll, which is inhabited by mysterious creatures – “Aniimo.” Players (nicknamed Pathfinders) are able to explore the vast continent, engage in action-based combat alone or in multiplayer, and befriend Aniimo. Much like in other creature collecting games, Aniimo each have their own “elements” attributed to them, as well as a 3-stage “evolution system.” According to the game’s official Wiki , some Aniimo also have different forms based on the environment they inhabit. On the other hand, one unique mechanic of the game is an ability called “Twining,” which lets you become any Aniimo from your party. This allows you to use their elemental abilities to solve puzzles or directly partake in combat.

The game was first announced in June 2025, with a closed beta test launching the following month. It went on to gather significant attention from online users, reaching over 30 million global pre-registrations over the course of a year. And now that it has finally launched, it has been showing record numbers of concurrent players.

According to SteamDB data (as of writing this article), Aniimo peaked at over 101,000 concurrent players in the first 3 hours since launch, and is currently ranked among the top 10 most played games on Steam. The actual number of concurrent players might be even larger considering the number of platforms that the game has launched on.

On the other hand, the game’s Steam version currently sits at a “Mixed” review score with 50% positive reviews out of a total of over 1,000 at the time of writing. Many of the negative reviews cite overly aggressive monetization, a slow gameplay loop, and improper controller optimization. Other reviews also note that many of the drawbacks of the beta version haven’t been addressed in the full version of the game. While it hasn’t been a day since the game released, it will be interesting to see if and how the developers will address these concerns in future updates.

Aniimo is currently for PC (Steam/Epic Games/official launcher), PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game will release for Android and iOS on September 23.

items.title: 5 Best Survival Games Of 2026 (So Far)
items.summary: 2026 has been a great year for video games in the survival genre, and we
items.content:
Iron Gate Studio Add SVG on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Survival games pit players against the elements, from adverse weather conditions to hostile wildlife and rival characters keeping gamers on the defensive. Resource management and crafting are often major mechanics within the genre, making players think strategically how to best proceed. There are differing levels of difficulty and intensity, of course, but it's these sensibilities that distinguish these gameplay experiences from typical action games.

2026 has been a particularly robust year as far as the release of new survival video games. From games officially emerging from early access to get their full release to indie gems that caught us by surprise, there are a lot of genre titles to choose from. We're highlighting some personal favorites, each getting to the heart of what survival games are about. Here are the five best survival games of 2026 so far, putting players to the test to make it out alive.

Pocketpair "Pokémon" has been a staple in the gaming industry for 30 years and led to a number of clone games that are actually great . This includes "Palworld," which began its early access period in 2024 before getting its full release this past July. The game feels like a dark parody of "Pokémon" with a survivalist twist as players have their recruited pals build up the homestead and train to use weapons. Not taking the joke in stride, Nintendo filed a lawsuit against "Palworld," but that wasn't enough to impede its eventual official release.

For fans who wanted "Pokémon" to have a more violent edge, "Palworld" certainly delivers on that score. The game mixes crafting and community-building gameplay with its expected monster-taming premise and decidedly dark sense of humor. But for all the notoriety that "Palword" earned from its idea of giving cutesy monsters guns, the gameplay is genuinely enjoyable. Far more than being the one-joke gimmick the buzz would have you believe, "Palworld" is worth giving a try.

Unknown Worlds Entertainment While most survival games take place on terra firma, the 2018 game "Subnautica" took its action to an extraterrestrial sea. The eagerly anticipated sequel "Subnautica 2" goes even deeper with its exploration and terrifying underwater encounters, while adding multiplayer. The game's story has players investigate what happened to a colony, searching for clues throughout a sweeping ocean on a faraway world. Players get new vehicles to explore underwater environments as well as the ability to alter their DNA to gain new abilities.

"Subnautica 2" is one of the best submarine games of all time , in no small part due to its deepened survivalist elements. The inclusion of cooperative multiplayer is a big leap up over its predecessor, especially when it comes to embarking on the immersive exploration. But more than anything else, the sheer scope and new sea life designs, including the usual frightening leviathans, is where the true fun lies. Bigger, better, and deeper than its predecessor, "Subnautica 2" feels like a truly more grandiose sequel.

Chilla's Art The Japanese indie studio Chilla's Art has been making lo-fi horror games for years, with standouts being "The Closing Shift" and "Parasocial." For the studio's latest release, "Snowed Under," the action turns more towards survivalist stakes — at least at first. The game opens with the protagonist and her friend sheltering in a remote cabin that's engulfed in a blizzard. Players must regularly tunnel through the snow to search for supplies, including scrap wood to maintain fires in order to stay warm at night.

Of course, being a Chilla's Art game, "Snowed Under" delves into supernatural horror territory as it progresses. But even with those horror elements in full display, the game is interesting enough at face value as players try to forage and stay alive for a long, frigid winter. As the paranormal terror becomes a more evident part of the story, players will want to be more careful where they dig or risk uncovering something they don't want to. A lo-fi thriller as only Chilla's Art could deliver, "Snowed Under" is best played with the lights out on a chilly night.

Iron Gate Studio Another game that saw a lengthy early access period before finally getting its official release this year is "Valheim." Developed by Iron Gate Studio, the game takes place in a Norse afterlife where slain Vikings prove themselves worthy to enter the warriors' paradise of Valhalla. Played from a third-person perspective, players create a homestead in this harsh open-world environment, foraging and crafting to boost their stamina and health. Players build up their skills while battling monsters throughout the ephemeral realm to showcase their worthiness.

Even before its full release, "Valheim" was a decided success , with millions of players checking it out. The game features gorgeous art design and its gameplay mechanics feel noticeably refined, improving with each update ahead of its official launch. While boasting an engaging single-player experience, the game also provides competitive and cooperative multiplayer modes to share the fun. Now fully on the market, "Valheim" has lived up to the promises of its early access period (and then some).

Keen Games Okay, "Enshrouded" is still technically in its early access period at the time of this writing, but its official release is a month away. Unless the game changes dramatically within that short timespan, which we don't see happening, it earns a spot on this list. A medieval fantasy game, the title takes place in an open-world map, with players able to dive in alone or with up to 15 other gamers. Players build up their homestead while venturing into the foggy surrounding areas, battling monsters and harvesting valuable loot to bring back and craft with.

While there is plenty of third-person hack-and-slash combat, the real appeal to "Enshrouded" is in its harvesting and crafting mechanics. So much of the joy in playing the game comes from obtaining new recipes and embarking on quests into dangerous areas to get the necessary ingredients. The game also features visibly moody environments to explore, leaning into the shadowy premise alluded to by its title. We've seen promising things from "Enshrouded" for the two years it has been in early access, and its full release looks to be even better.

items.title: This New Survival Game Finally Clicked with Me, and I'm Never Looking Back
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 does a great job of easing you into its many complex systems.
items.content:
Survival games have been wildly popular for years now. I’ve dabbled here and there to see what the fuss is about, but I’ve always fallen off after a few hours. Usually, I get tangled up in one meagerly explained system after another until I lose track of what I’m supposed to do, and my time with the game peters out.

When Palworld 1.0 came out to rave reviews , I figured I’d give the genre another shot – and I’m glad I did. Palworld’s gradual, newbie-friendly onboarding helped me see what a whole lot of people have loved about survival games all along. Palworld made me a believer.

I’m glad I came in at the 1.0 mark, because I’ve heard Palworld had a much steeper learning curve out of the gate. But now, new players start with a series of missions designed to guide you through the game’s numerous systems . You learn how to punch trees to get wood to create a crafting bench. You learn how to make a club you can use to beat some Pals to death (it’s a dog-eat-dog world out there) to get wool. You then use that wool to make clothes. You set up a camp. You build a house. You activate a teleporter and explore deeper into the game world.

Before long, you’re gliding off cliffs Zelda-style before whomping on every Pal you see to catch them in spheres to put them to work. You can deploy them at your camp, ride them , or have them fight by your side to take on big roaming Pals and towering bosses . It’s a blast. And there’s no way I would have stuck with it if it hadn’t held my hand and eased me into the systems that make up the game.

I still have a long way to go, because I was nowhere near powerful enough to defeat the first boss solo. But those early missions gave me a much-needed handle on what else I can spend my time doing as I level up enough to become a threat. There's a vast world out there I can keep exploring, all while catching Pals and building up my base. I’m having a blast doing it.

Palworld’s 1.0 is available on Steam , Xbox , and PS5 . It costs $29.99, but you can save a few bucks on a Steam copy at Fanatical , which is currently running its summer sale .

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

items.title: Palworld 1.0 Review – Bigger, Better, and Still Brutally Addictive
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 is crammed with new content. More Pals, better quests, and a fully realized world for new and returning players to explore.
items.content:
Remember Palworld ? Well, the controversial game from Pocketpair finally has a 1.0 release. After two years, this feels like a very different animal than the one I initially encountered. The quest system is more complete, the UI is polished, and the world feels much more interconnected than before. While there are still some rough edges, this version of Palworld is a vastly improved one.

Now, I haven’t been keeping up with every iteration of Palworld released up to this point. So I’m not clear on how gradual or sudden these changes might be. But oh man, the quest system feels like night and day. You’re fed a steady stream of quests from the jump. They pair nicely with the tech tree, they appear on your map, and they sync with your compass. Yes, this is incredibly basic stuff. We figured out quest design decades ago. But you really appreciate the elegance of that design when it’s missing. Then when it finally shows up? It’s water in the desert.

Beyond the quests, it turns out Palworld works much better with connective tissue in place. Fast travel points, side quests, a detailed map, and distant objectives (like a floating island on the horizon) all make the world feel more tangible. Having an objective at all times kept me hooked on the game. Or at least, objectives are perfect for stringing you along until the factory sim element gets its claws in you. Once the big machine gets going, you don’t need anything else to maintain momentum.

The complete list of additions in Palworld 1.0 is downright intimidating. You can read the whole thing on their Steam page, but the highlights are remarkable. 72 new Pals, the Sunreach region, the World Tree, and an increased level cap all speak to a much larger, more complete game. There’s more of course, but the point remains – Palworld has undergone significant changes since the early access days.

This new version of Palworld still has some flaws, to be fair. The laptop I’m using is decently powerful, but I encountered a handful of framerate dips regardless. More important than the tiny performance issues is the core gameplay loop. Things hum along at a more relatable pace than ever before, sure. But you’re still faced with a pretty murderous grind. Pal levels creep upward slowly, and getting through that tech trees gets daunting quite quickly. While things start out breezy enough, the endgame is strictly for simulation psychopaths.

By which I mean the truly dedicated. Which is totally fine! There’s a fascinating disconnect between the monster battling and the base building. You can immerse yourself in one and ignore the other, at least for a hefty chunk of playtime. Although perhaps my impressions of the battling are skewed by hands off it all is. Your Pals run on autopilot, both in battle and beyond it. So for me, the fights are a diversion from my tiny empire.

In that regard, Palworld remains a specialized interest. Either you’re ready to get lost in the details of empire expansion and monster murder, or you’ll quickly lose momentum. The quest system, new content, and expanded Pal roster are all incidental in the face of this essential truth. The gooey caramel center that is the gameplay loop is more or less the same as it ever was. My mind was changed about this game, true. But I’m prone to hyper focus and bouts of mania. So a vast and ruthless machine like Palworld is straight up catnip for my badly wired brain.

The 1.0 release of Palworld presents a very different game than the original early access version. The quest system has been revamped, the map has been expanded, and civilization is scattered everywhere. But the gameplay loop is still pretty relentless. Plus, the rough edges haven’t been completely removed. If the old game was almost it for you, this new iteration might be exactly what you yearned for. But Palworld 1.0 is still an acquired taste.

***A Steam key was provided by the publisher***

} .login #login, .login #lostpasswordform { min-width: 350px !important; } .wpforms-field-c4wp iframe { width: 100% !important; } ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Entertainment Lists MMA NHL Soccer Tennis Video Games Watch WNBA WWE Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube Linkedin Palworld review: Fresh and innovative, despite appearances By Ryan Woodrow | July 22, 2026 Photo Credit: Pocketpair When Palworld first launched into early access two and a half years ago, I described it as a “breath of fresh air” for the survival-crafting genre, and in the time since then, the state of that genre hasn’t changed. I still find it to be one of the most stagnant genres out there, with a formula that I once found enjoyable when Minecraft and Terraria stumbled upon it, but has now been worn into the ground by every early access game on Steam.

That’s why I was so surprised how much creature collecting adds to that formula, but now the game has hit 1.0 and officially launched, I can see it goes a lot deeper than just slapping a couple hundred colorful creatures on top of the standard survival-crafting affair.

The Pals that roam the world aren’t just set dressing or collectibles; they’re integral to every single part of the core loop. Upon defeating or catching them, you get resources vital to progression that can’t be obtained through any other means; catching them is your main source of EXP, which is how you progress through the game’s tech tree; and most importantly, you can put the Pals to work at your base to complete tasks for you.

While the trailers for the game present this as a funny, edgy thing where they’re emphasizing the darker elements of the world that Pokémon likes to gloss over, putting Pals to work is a vital part of the game, and a surprisingly deep system.

There are 12 different work suitabilities that determine what tasks a Pal can perform. This includes things like planting, crafting, smelting, watering, and a bunch more, and each one has levels from 0 to 10 showing how quickly they’ll perform the task. This means that, as your base grows, finding the right balance of Pal proficiencies is vital to making meaningful progress, especially as, once you get out of the early game, there are many things that you won’t be able to do yourself.

Source: Pocketpair Take smelting, for example. You can’t just slap some coal in a furnace and wait for everything to cook; you have to get a fire Pal to cook it for you, and as you go up each tier of material, you’re going to need to find Pals that are much better at that task to get it done in a reasonable time frame.

And that’s all without taking into account the passive and partner skill systems, where every species of Pal has a unique partner skill, and every single Pal you catch has a random selection of passives that either help or hinder their work. It makes you actually care deeply about your Pals, as you’re paying attention to their every detail. While in Pokémon, you only have to worry about breeding and traits if you want to play competitively, in Palworld, that stuff is baked into the foundation of the singleplayer experience.

Not to mention, it also helps build the world, the lore, and the characters of the Pals. While some partner skills will be passive boosts, there are some Pal duos, like Anubis and Sehkmet, that specifically boost each other when working together, giving you another layer of considerations to make when organizing your base.

If that all sounds complicated, it really isn’t, as the game makes it very easy to manage. Early on, you’ll unlock a podium that lets you assign Pals to specific tasks, as well as dictate which of their proficiencies they are and aren’t allowed to use when unassigned, to ensure that everyone focuses on the jobs you intend for them.

But all of these Pals don’t just wander in unannounced; you have to seek them out in the world, which is Palworld’s other great strength: the exploration.

With an impressive draw distance, as soon as you walk out into the world, you’ll spot all kinds of wondrous sights. Volcanoes, snow mountains, lush forests, and even oil rigs all litter the landscape, and if you can see it, you can go there. The only restriction is the World Tree, which is locked behind endgame progression, but even that makes for a tantalizing mystery constantly on the horizon that you’re working towards.

Source: Pocketpair You settle into a well-paced loop where you work improving your base for a while, which in turn improves your gear so you can then go and explore further afield into higher-level areas with brand new Pals to catch, boosting your EXP and giving you new resources to help you progress even further when you return to base. It’s a simple loop, but one that so many survival-crafting games fail to implement satisfyingly; that’s the power of a creature collector.

So let’s talk about the Pals themselves, because with 204 unique designs and 278 total designs when you include hybrids – which are elemental variants on existing Pals that only vary in color – there are honestly very few misses among the pack. There are a handful of basic ones you probably won’t give much thought to, but the vast majority of Pals have a tangible charisma to their designs that makes them compelling.

I actually found the game’s five-Pal party quite restrictive considering how many cool designs there were that I wanted to use on my team, though this is where having many slots at your base for workers helps, as you do form relationships with those Pals too.
